issues.issue: The grant of the right to transport oil and gas "from the subject and other lands" across the leasehold, surviving the lease term, cannot be squared with paragraph 25, which says the Lessee will not assert a right to transport production from other lands unless the premises are pooled, or with Addendum paragraph 20 denying any right to move foreign gas across the premises. A court would have to decide which grant governs.

The habendum extension turns on gas being "produced or capable of being produced on the premises in paying quantities, in the judgment of the Lessee" — both "paying quantities" and the Lessee's own "judgment" are undefined and carry more than one reasonable meaning. Whether mere capability, judged subjectively, holds the lease is genuinely open.

The clause extends the term "as provided in Paragraph 7 following," but Paragraph 7 concerns adequacy of consideration and drilling discretion; it is Paragraph 6 (shut-in royalty) that bears on holding the lease without marketed production. The cross-reference cannot be reconciled with the paragraph it points to.
"A well shall be deemed commenced when preparations for drilling have been commenced" leaves "preparations for drilling" wholly undefined, so almost any site activity could qualify.

Addendum paragraph 16 defines commencement of operations as entering with equipment to build access roads followed by a drilling rig for spudding, a narrower test than this paragraph's "preparations for drilling," and the Addendum priority clause makes the Addendum prevail. The two definitions must be reconciled.

The royalty in (B) is one-eighth of "the price paid to Lessee," followed by a struck-through post-production-cost deduction clause; whether the deletion bars deductions, and what "price paid to Lessee" means at what point of sale, is exactly the kind of question two parties read differently. The (A) "free of cost" language and (C)'s mandatory tax deduction pull in different directions within the same paragraph.

Payment is to be made to "LESSOR at ABOVE ADDRESS" and "the said named person shall continue as Lessor's agent," but this lease names four separate lessors at four addresses, so no single "said named person" is identified. The designated payee is indeterminate on the face of the clause.

The clause fixes a shut-in payment but never says the payment maintains the lease, which must be read against paragraph 2's habendum requiring production "in paying quantities" or capability of production. Whether shut-in payments hold the lease past the primary term is left open.

This paragraph gives the Lessee "the further right of drilling or not drilling ... as the Lessee may elect," while paragraph 8 states the Lessee "shall be required to maintain a well density of at least 1 well per 160 acres" in a unit. The unfettered election and the mandatory density cannot both be given full effect.

"Lessee shall be required to maintain a well density of at least 1 well per 160 acres contained in such [unit]" is susceptible of being read either as an affirmative drilling obligation or as a cap on unit size, and "maintain" fixes no time by which the density must exist. The sentence as printed even refers to acres contained "in such well."

The well-density requirement sits against paragraph 7, which reserves to the Lessee "the further right of drilling or not drilling ... as the Lessee may elect," and paragraph 20, which forbids reading any implied covenant into the lease. A court must decide whether the density sentence imposes a duty those clauses deny.

This paragraph has the Lessor waive "notice of any assignment or transfer of the within lease," but Addendum paragraph 17 obliges the Lessee to give written notice of any assignment of a 51% or greater interest within fourteen days, and the Addendum is stated to prevail. The waiver and the notice duty conflict.

"Any damages if not mutually agreed upon" are to go to three appraisers and "Arbitration shall be mandatory," but the clause never says which damages are covered — only crop and drainage damages are enumerated — nor whether the appraisal is an arbitration for enforcement purposes. The scope of the mandatory process is uncertain.

The Lessor must abide by "all reasonable safety policies of Lessee ... including but not limited to" a single enumerated setback rule, so the general catch-all's reach beyond the one specific is undefined and the Lessee alone fixes the policies. This is a classic general-versus-specific problem.

On surrender "the land rental hereinbefore set forth shall be reduced in proportion to the acreage surrendered," but paragraph 3 declares this a "paid up bonus lease" and no delay rental is set forth anywhere in the instrument. The reduction mechanism has no referent in the rest of the lease.

"Force majeure, including but not limited to acts of God, strikes, riots and governmental restrictions" leaves the catch-all's reach beyond the enumerated items undefined, and the closing words — the lease shall not expire "for a period of ninety (90) days after the termination of any force majeure" — are ambiguous as to whether the extension is ninety days or indefinite.

The Lessee need only "meet or commence to meet all or any part of the breaches alleged" within thirty days, a standard that does not say what suffices to cure or how much of a breach must be addressed. Whether merely commencing satisfies the condition precedent to suit is open.

The extension option runs "for one additional primary term of ___ commencing on the date that the lease would have expired," with the length of the extended term left blank on the face of the clause. The duration of the extension cannot be determined from the writing.

The integration clause and the bar on reading any "implied covenant, agreement or obligation" into the lease must be squared with the Addendum, which is incorporated by paragraph 26 and declared to supersede inconsistent main-body terms. Whether the merger language limits the Addendum's operation is a live question.

This paragraph covers Clean and Green assessments, while Addendum paragraph 13 covers the same subject in different terms (adding CREP and, as printed, directing payment of fines "levied against the Lessee"). The two provisions overlap imperfectly and the Addendum is stated to prevail.

This paragraph requires locations to be fixed by "mutual consent," with the Lessor's consent not to be unreasonably withheld, whereas Addendum paragraph 3 deems the Lessor to have approved a location if he fails to return the approval form within thirty days. Deemed approval and mutual consent are not the same regime.

The promise not to assert a right to transport gas from other lands across the premises unless the lands are pooled contradicts the paragraph 1 grant, which expressly conveys that transport right "regardless of the source of such production" and makes it survive the lease term. Addendum paragraph 20 states the prohibition even more absolutely.

The priority clause operates only on an "inconsistency" between the Addendum and the main body, and the instrument contains several candidates — Addendum paragraph 20 against paragraph 1's transport grant, Addendum paragraph 16 against paragraph 3, Addendum paragraph 17 against paragraph 11's notice waiver. Identifying which terms are inconsistent is itself a construction question.

Restoration "as nearly as possible" to the pre-drilling condition, to be completed "within 90 days, weather permitting," sets no measurable standard and the weather proviso has no boundary. Both the standard and the deadline are open-ended.

Restoration to "as near its original condition as is reasonably possible" is a different and looser standard than Addendum paragraph 1's "as nearly as possible" and carries no deadline. Which standard governs, and what it requires, is left to argument.

The deemed-approval mechanism (silence for thirty days constitutes approval) is difficult to reconcile with main-body paragraph 23, which requires locations to be fixed by "mutual consent" between Lessor and Lessee. A court would have to decide whether silence can supply the mutual consent that paragraph 23 demands.

The provision survives only as the fragment "caused by any actions or omissions," so its operative subject, scope and beneficiary cannot be determined from the text. What indemnity, if any, was agreed is unascertainable on the face of it.

The covenant that the Lessee acquires no right to drill an underground gas or oil storage well conflicts with the paragraph 1 grant of the right of "injecting and storing, air, gas, brine and other substances from any source and into any subsurface strata." The scope of the storage exclusion against that grant is genuinely contestable.

The trigger is a "material adverse change in the quality of Lessor's water supply" occurring "during or immediately after the completion" of drilling, neither of which is defined or bounded in time. Both the materiality threshold and the window are open to competing readings.

The paragraph promises the Lessee will pay the additional costs, taxes, penalties and fines "so levied against the Lessee," although the whole premise of the clause is that the taxing authority has assessed them against the Lessor. As written the obligation is self-referential and pays nothing to the Lessor.

This definition of commencement — entry with equipment to build access roads followed by a drilling rig for spudding — is narrower than main-body paragraph 3, under which a well is "deemed commenced when preparations for drilling have been commenced." The two tests give different answers on the same facts.

The duty to give written notice of any assignment of a 51% or greater interest conflicts with main-body paragraph 11, in which "Lessor waives notice of any assignment or transfer of the within lease." Whether notice is owed at all turns on which clause governs.

The location fee is written as "Two and Five Hundred (2,500.00) dollars," so the words and the figure do not correspond and the amount payable is not determinable from the text. The trigger, "upon commencement of drilling operations," also depends on which commencement definition applies.

The paragraph opens "Lessor does not acquire ... the right to transport foreign gas across the premises," which reverses the parties and makes the sentence meaningless; the intended subject is plainly the Lessee. "Foreign gas" is also nowhere defined.

The denial of any right to move foreign gas across the premises squarely contradicts paragraph 1, which grants the right to transport oil and gas "from the subject and other lands ... regardless of the source of such production" and makes that right survive the term. Paragraph 25 permits such transport once the lands are pooled, which this paragraph does not.
